fields.title: 2 Chronicles
fields.subtitle: Divrei HaYamim Bet, “The events of the days”
fields.description: The second half of Chronicles and, in most Hebrew Bibles, the last book of the Old Testament. Solomon builds the temple, and as the singers praise the LORD the house is filled with the cloud of glory; then God answers his prayer: “if my people who bear my name humble themselves and pray, seek my face and turn back from their evil ways, then I myself will hear from heaven.” The kings of Judah follow, each a lesson in seeking God or forsaking him: Asa’s cry for help, Jehoshaphat’s singers marching ahead of the army, Hezekiah’s Passover for the unclean, Manasseh praying in chains in Babylon, Josiah weeping over the book of the law. It ends with the temple in ashes and a Persian king’s decree: “let them go up.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of 2 Chronicles?
qa.answer: The second half of Chronicles, which in Hebrew is a single book called Divrei HaYamim, “the events of the days”. Its thirty-six chapters tell of Solomon and the building of the temple (1–9) and then of the kings of Judah, the line of David, from the division of the kingdom around 930 BC to the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon in 586 BC, ending with the decree of Cyrus king of Persia in 538 BC that allowed the exiles to return and rebuild. In most Hebrew Bibles it is the last book of the Old Testament.

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Chronicles, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited Chronicles to Ezra the scribe, and its last two verses are repeated at the beginning of the book of Ezra. Many scholars speak simply of “the Chronicler”, writing after the exile, in the Persian period, perhaps around 400 BC; some date it earlier. Whether the same writer produced Ezra and Nehemiah is debated. The book names many sources, among them the records of prophets such as Nathan, Iddo, Shemaiah and Isaiah.

qa.question: What does 2 Chronicles 7:14 mean?
qa.answer: It is God’s answer to Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple: when God sends drought, locusts or plague, “if my people who bear my name humble themselves and pray, seek my face and turn back from their evil ways, then I myself will hear from heaven. I will forgive their sin and heal their land.” It was first spoken to Israel and tied to prayer made toward the temple (7:15). Christians differ on how directly it applies to modern nations, but have widely taken its pattern of humbling, praying, seeking and turning as God’s way with his people, and the rest of 2 Chronicles shows that pattern at work in king after king.

qa.question: Why does 2 Chronicles leave out the kings of Israel?
qa.answer: Chronicles tells the story of the line of David and the temple in Jerusalem, so it follows the kings of Judah and mentions the northern kingdom only where its history touches Judah’s. It was written for the community that returned from exile, who were descended mainly from Judah and gathered around the rebuilt temple. Yet it never writes the northern tribes off: it shows Hezekiah inviting the remnant of Israel to his Passover and some of them coming to Jerusalem, and it counts all twelve tribes as Israel.

qa.question: Did King Manasseh repent?
qa.answer: According to 2 Chronicles 33:10–17, yes. 2 Kings presents Manasseh as the worst of Judah’s kings, but Chronicles adds that after the Assyrians took him to Babylon in chains, “he sought the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself deeply”, and God heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem, where he removed the foreign gods from the temple. The two accounts are usually read together: Kings stresses the lasting harm of his reign, and Chronicles the mercy of God to a repentant sinner. The Prayer of Manasseh found in some Bibles is a later work, not part of the Hebrew text.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
and if my people who bear my name humble themselves and pray, seek my face and turn back from their evil ways, then I myself will hear from heaven. I will forgive their sin and heal their land.

— 2 Chronicles 7:14

2 Chronicles begins with a young king asking God for wisdom and ends with a pagan emperor telling God’s people to go home. In between, it tells the story of Judah’s kings over four centuries, from Solomon’s temple filled with glory to the same temple in ashes, and it tells it as a long lesson in what happens when people seek God, and when they do not.

It is the second half of the book called in Hebrew Divrei HaYamim, “the events of the days”, divided in two by the ancient Greek translation. It runs from about 970 BC to 538 BC, the first year of Cyrus king of Persia. In most Hebrew Bibles it is the last book of all, and its last words are a king’s proclamation to the scattered people of God: “let them go up.” The Hebrew Scriptures end not with a full stop but with an open door.

The shape of the book

Chapters 1–9 tell of Solomon, and above all of the temple he built. Chapters 10–36 follow the kings of Judah, the descendants of David, from the division of the kingdom to the exile in Babylon. The northern kingdom of Israel, which fills so many pages of Kings, appears only where it touches Judah; for Chronicles, the line of God’s promise runs through David’s house and Jerusalem’s temple. Yet the book never forgets the northern tribes, and more than once it shows Judah’s kings inviting them home.

The story is told with great freedom. Some reigns that take pages in Kings are summarised in a few lines, and others are greatly enlarged, especially those of four reforming kings: Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah. Much of what Chronicles adds is preaching and prayer. Prophets appear again and again, many of them unknown from any other book, and kings pray long prayers before battles and festivals. The writer is not only reporting what happened. He is showing his readers how to live.

Solomon and the glory

Solomon begins his reign by asking, as in 1 Kings, for wisdom rather than riches: “Now give me wisdom and knowledge, so that I may go out and come in before this people as their leader.” He builds the temple “on Mount Moriah”, on the threshing floor David bought from Ornan, and Chronicles lingers over its gold, its bronze pillars and its furnishings.

The high point comes at the dedication. The priests have brought the ark into the inner room; the Levite singers in fine linen stand by the altar with cymbals, harps and lyres, and a hundred and twenty priests with trumpets:

The trumpeters and the singers joined as one, making a single sound heard as they praised and thanked the LORD. As they raised the sound with trumpets, cymbals and other musical instruments and praised the LORD, “For he is good; his loyal love lasts forever,” the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud, and the priests were unable to stand and do their service because of the cloud, since the house of God was full of the glory of the LORD.

— 2 Chronicles 5:13–14

In Chronicles the glory comes while the people are singing the refrain David gave them. Solomon prays the great prayer of dedication, asking, “But will God really live on earth with human beings?”, and when he finishes, “fire came down from heaven and devoured the burnt offering”, and the people kneel with their faces to the pavement and give thanks, “for he is good; his loyal love lasts forever.”

Chronicles does not tell of the many wives who turned Solomon’s heart away; it leaves him at the height of his glory, greater “in riches and in wisdom than all the kings of the earth.” That is not ignorance of Kings, which its readers knew well, but a choice to remember Solomon as the builder of the house of prayer.

“If my people…”

After the dedication the LORD appears to Solomon by night, and answers his prayer with the promise that heads this introduction. Its setting matters: it is God’s reply to Solomon’s request that he would hear prayers made toward the temple in times of drought, locusts or plague. “When I shut up the sky so that no rain falls,” God says, and then, if his people humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from their evil ways, he will hear, forgive and heal.

Many Christians have prayed this verse for their own countries. Others point out that it was spoken to Israel, the people who bore God’s name, and was tied to “the prayer made in this place”. Both are worth hearing: the promise was first Israel’s, and yet the pattern it describes is God’s way with his people in every age, and the church, which also bears his name, has rightly taken it to heart.

In any case, the rest of 2 Chronicles is a kind of commentary on this verse. Its four verbs, humble, pray, seek and turn, come back again and again, and so does God’s response. When king and officials humble themselves under Rehoboam, the word comes, “They have humbled themselves, so I will not destroy them.” When Hezekiah prays for people who are not ritually clean, “The LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.”

Seeking and finding

Asa’s reign is the first full illustration. Faced with a vast army from Cush, he prays one of the great short prayers of the Bible: “LORD, there is no one but you to help when the weak stand against the strong. Help us, LORD our God, because we are depending on you” (14:11). After the victory, a prophet named Azariah meets him with a word that could stand over the whole book:

He went out to meet Asa and spoke to him: “Hear me, Asa, and all of Judah and Benjamin. The LORD is with you as long as you are with him. If you seek him, he will let you find him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you.

— 2 Chronicles 15:2

Asa and the people enter a covenant to seek the LORD “with all their heart and with all their soul”, and “he let them find him. So the LORD gave them rest on every side.” But late in his reign, threatened by the northern kingdom, Asa pays the king of Aram to rescue him instead of trusting God, and the seer Hanani rebukes him:

For the eyes of the LORD roam over all the earth, so that he may show his strength for those whose hearts are undivided toward him. You have acted foolishly in this matter, and from this time on you will face wars.”

— 2 Chronicles 16:9

Asa jails the prophet. In his last illness, the book says, “he did not seek the LORD; he sought only the physicians.” The point is not that doctors are wrong, but that Asa, who once prayed so well, had come to rely on anything but God.

Jehoshaphat: “the battle is not yours”

Asa’s son Jehoshaphat sends officials and Levites through the towns of Judah, “having the book of the law of the LORD with them”, to teach the people. He appoints judges and tells them, “the LORD our God does no wrong, plays no favorites and takes no bribe.” He is rebuked for his alliance with Ahab, but his great moment comes when a coalition of Moab, Ammon and others invades. Jehoshaphat “resolved to seek the LORD”, proclaims a fast, and stands before the people in the temple to pray. His prayer ends with one of the most honest sentences in Scripture:

Our God, will you not judge them? We have no strength to face this great army that is coming against us. We have no idea what we should do, but our eyes are turned toward you.”

— 2 Chronicles 20:12

The Spirit comes on a Levite named Jahaziel, who tells them, “the battle is not yours; it belongs to God.” The next morning Jehoshaphat sends the singers out ahead of the army, praising the LORD, and tells the people, “Hold firm in your trust in the LORD your God, and you will be held firm.” The Hebrew is a play on a single word, to believe and to be made firm, which Alexander Maclaren made the subject of a sermon. As the singing begins, the invaders turn on one another.

Good beginnings, bad endings

Again and again Chronicles shows kings who start well and finish badly. Joash, the boy king saved from Athaliah, “did what was right in the sight of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.” After Jehoiada dies, he lets his officials lead him back to idols. When Jehoiada’s son Zechariah warns them, “Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has forsaken you,” they stone him in the temple courtyard at the king’s command. His last words are, “May the LORD see this and call you to account!” Jesus remembered him. He spoke of the blood of the prophets “from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who died between the altar and the house of God” (Luke 11:51); since Chronicles stands last in the Hebrew Bible, many readers take him to mean the first murder and the last in the Scriptures.

Amaziah “did what was right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a whole heart.” Uzziah, who sought God in the days of his teacher Zechariah, prospered, “for he was wonderfully helped until he became strong.” Then “his heart grew proud, to his own ruin”, and he went into the temple to burn incense, a duty only the priests could do, and left it with a serious skin disease he carried to his death. The danger in Chronicles is rarely weakness. It is strength that forgets where it came from.

There are surprises of mercy, too. When the army of the northern kingdom carries off thousands of captives from Judah, a prophet named Oded meets them at Samaria and tells them to send their own relatives home. They clothe the captives from the plunder, give them food and drink, anoint them with oil, put the weak on donkeys and bring them to Jericho (28:15). Many readers have heard in it an echo of the parable of the Good Samaritan.

Hezekiah opens the doors

Ahaz, Hezekiah’s father, had shut the doors of the temple. In the first month of his reign, Hezekiah “opened the doors of the house of the LORD and made them strong again.” Chronicles gives three chapters to his reforms, and most of all to a Passover, to which he invites not only Judah but the remnant of the northern tribes. His couriers carry letters as far as Zebulun: “Israelites, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, and he will return to those of you who are left.” Most of the north laughs at them; some humble themselves and come.

Many of those who come have not been purified as the law required, and they eat the Passover anyway. Hezekiah does not turn them away. He prays:

A large part of the people, many of them from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun, had not purified themselves, and yet they ate the Passover in a way that did not keep to what is written. But Hezekiah prayed for them, saying, “May the LORD, who is good, pardon everyone who sets their heart on seeking God, the LORD, the God of their ancestors, even if they are not clean as the sanctuary requires.”

— 2 Chronicles 30:18–19

“The LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.” It is the promise of 7:14 kept. When Sennacherib invades, Hezekiah tells the people, “With him is only an arm of flesh, but we have the LORD our God with us.” And when his heart grows proud after his recovery from illness, he humbles himself too.

Manasseh

The greatest surprise in Chronicles is the story of Manasseh. In Kings he is the worst of Judah’s kings, whose sins sealed the city’s fate. Chronicles tells the same evil, but then something Kings does not: the Assyrians take him to Babylon with hooks and bronze chains, and there:

In his distress he sought the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself deeply before the God of his ancestors. He prayed to him, and he was moved by his prayer. He heard his plea for mercy and brought him back to Jerusalem, to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God.

— 2 Chronicles 33:12–13

He comes home, removes the foreign gods from the temple and restores the altar of the LORD. Readers have asked how this fits with Kings. The two accounts need not conflict: Kings is concerned with the harm Manasseh did, which outlived him, and Chronicles with what God did for Manasseh. For the exiles who first read it, his story meant that no one was beyond repentance, not even a king who had led a whole nation into evil. A short prayer in his name, the Prayer of Manasseh, was later composed and is printed among the Apocrypha in some Bibles; it is not part of the Hebrew text.

Josiah, and the end

Of Josiah, Manasseh’s grandson, the book says that “while he was still young, he began to seek the God of his ancestor David.” He purges the land, repairs the temple, hears the book of the law, renews the covenant and keeps a Passover unequalled “since the days of Samuel the prophet”. But he dies at Megiddo, and Chronicles adds a sobering detail: he went out against Pharaoh Neco after “He did not listen to Neco’s words, which came from the mouth of God.” Even the best king could fail to listen.

Then the end comes quickly, and Chronicles explains it in some of the most moving sentences in the Old Testament:

The LORD, the God of their ancestors, sent word to them through his messengers again and again, because he felt compassion for his people and for his dwelling place. But they made fun of God’s messengers, scorned his words and sneered at his prophets, until the fury of the LORD rose up against his people and nothing could heal them.

— 2 Chronicles 36:15–16

The temple is burned and the people taken to Babylon. Yet even the exile is given a meaning: the land keeps its Sabbaths, “until seventy years were complete”, as Jeremiah had said. The years of loss are years of rest. And then the LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus, and the book ends with an invitation.

How to read 2 Chronicles

Read it beside 1 and 2 Kings, which tell much of the same story, and notice what Chronicles adds: the prophets’ words, the kings’ prayers, the singers and the festivals. Follow its key words, seek, humble, rely and whole heart. Chronicles often shows faithfulness rewarded and unfaithfulness punished within a king’s own lifetime. Some readers find this too tidy; others note that the writer is teaching a pattern, not claiming that all suffering is deserved, and that he is just as insistent on mercy for those who humble themselves.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credited Chronicles to Ezra, and its last two verses are repeated at the start of the book of Ezra; many scholars speak simply of “the Chronicler”, writing in the Persian period, perhaps around 400 BC. Some numbers differ from those in Kings: Jehoiachin is eighteen when he becomes king in 2 Kings 24:8 and eight in 2 Chronicles 36:9, a difference most explain as an error in copying. Christians hold a range of views on such details.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 2 Chronicles are worth knowing.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation follows long custom and writes “the LORD”.

“He will let you find him.” The Hebrew of Azariah’s promise says literally that God “will be found by you”. This translation renders it “he will let you find him”, making clear that finding God is his gift.

“Held firm.” Jehoshaphat’s words in 20:20 play on one Hebrew root, to trust and to be made firm, and the translation keeps the play: “Hold firm in your trust in the LORD your God, and you will be held firm.”

“Loyal love.” The refrain sung at the temple and on the march, “his loyal love lasts forever”, renders the Hebrew hesed, God’s steadfast covenant love.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 1
fields.body_html:
Solomon asks for wisdom

1Solomon son of David established himself firmly over his kingdom. The LORD his God was with him and made him very great. 2Solomon addressed all Israel: the commanders over thousands and over hundreds, the judges, and every leader in all Israel, the heads of families. 3Then Solomon and the whole assembly with him went to the high place at Gibeon, because God’s tent of meeting was there, the one that Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness. 4But David had brought the ark of God up from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared, because he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem. 5Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, had made the bronze altar and set it in front of the tabernacle of the LORD, and there Solomon and the assembly sought him. 6There Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the LORD at the tent of meeting, and he offered up a thousand burnt offerings on it. 7That night God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Ask for whatever you want me to give you.” 8Solomon said to God, “You showed great faithful love to my father David, and you have put me on the throne in his place. 9Now, LORD God, let your promise to my father David prove true, since you have made me king over a people as many as the dust of the earth. 10Now give me wisdom and knowledge, so that I may go out and come in before this people as their leader. For who can judge this great people of yours?”

11God said to Solomon, “Because this was what your heart desired, and you have not asked for wealth, riches or honor, or the death of those who hate you, or even for a long life, but have asked for wisdom and knowledge so that you can judge my people over whom I have made you king, 12wisdom and knowledge are given to you. I will also give you wealth, riches and honor such as no king before you has had, and none after you will have.” 13Then Solomon left the tent of meeting at the high place in Gibeon and came back to Jerusalem, and he reigned over Israel.

Solomon’s horses and chariots

14Solomon built up a force of chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, which he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. 15The king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stones, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore-fig trees of the Shephelah. 16Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from Kue; the king’s traders bought them from Kue at the going price. 17They would import a chariot from Egypt for about 15 pounds of silver, and a horse for about 3 3/4 pounds. In the same way they exported them, through the king’s traders, to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram.
fields.summary: At Gibeon Solomon asks God for wisdom and knowledge to lead the people, and God gives him wealth and honor as well.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 2
fields.body_html:
Preparing to build the temple

1Solomon decided to build a house for the name of the LORD, and a palace for his own reign. 2Solomon assigned 70,000 men to carry loads and 80,000 men to cut stone in the hill country, and 3,600 to supervise them.

3Solomon sent this message to Huram king of Tyre: “Deal with me as you dealt with my father David, when you supplied him with cedar for building a house to live in. 4I am now going to build a house for the name of the LORD my God and dedicate it to him, for burning fragrant incense before him, for setting out the bread in rows regularly, and for burnt offerings every morning and evening, on Sabbaths, at new moons and at the appointed feasts of the LORD our God. This is a duty Israel is to keep forever. 5The house I am building will be great, because our God is great above all gods. 6But who is able to build a house for him, when heaven itself, even the highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I, then, to build him a house, except as a place to burn offerings before him? 7So now send me a man skilled in working with gold, silver, bronze and iron, and with purple, crimson and blue yarn, who also knows how to engrave. He will work with the skilled craftsmen I have here in Judah and Jerusalem, whom my father David provided. 8Send me cedar, cypress and algum logs from Lebanon too, for I know that your servants are skilled at cutting the timber of Lebanon. My servants will work with your servants, 9to get plenty of timber ready for me, because the house I am going to build will be great and wonderful. 10I will give your servants, the woodsmen who cut the timber, about 120,000 bushels of crushed wheat, about 120,000 bushels of barley, about 120,000 gallons of wine and about 120,000 gallons of oil.”

Huram’s reply

11Huram king of Tyre answered in a letter that he sent to Solomon: “Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you their king.” 12Huram also said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, maker of heaven and earth, who has given King David a wise son, full of insight and understanding, who will build a house for the LORD and a royal palace for himself. 13I am now sending you a skilled man who has understanding, Huram-abi, 14the son of a woman from the tribe of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre. He is trained to work in gold and silver, bronze and iron, stone and wood, and in purple, blue and crimson yarn and fine linen. He can engrave any kind of design and carry out any plan that is given to him. He will work with your craftsmen and with the craftsmen of my lord David, your father. 15So now let my lord send his servants the wheat and barley, the oil and wine, that he has promised. 16We will cut all the logs you need from Lebanon and bring them to you as rafts by sea to Joppa. From there you can take them up to Jerusalem.”

17Solomon took a census of all the outsiders who lived in the land of Israel, after the one his father David had taken, and they came to 153,600. 18He assigned 70,000 of them to carry loads and 80,000 to cut stone in the hill country, and 3,600 to supervise them and keep the people at work.
fields.summary: Solomon prepares to build the temple and asks Huram king of Tyre for cedar and a skilled craftsman.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 3
fields.body_html:
Solomon builds the temple

1In Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, Solomon began building the house of the LORD. It was there that the LORD had appeared to his father David, at the site David had prepared, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. 2He began to build in the fourth year of his reign, on the second day of the second month. 3These are the measurements Solomon laid down for building the house of God: measured by the old standard, the length was about 90 feet and the width about 30 feet. 4The porch in front of the temple was about 30 feet long, matching the width of the temple, and about 180 feet high. He overlaid its inside with pure gold. 5He paneled the main hall with cypress wood and overlaid it with fine gold, and he decorated it with palm trees and chains. 6He adorned the temple with precious stones to make it beautiful, and the gold he used was gold from Parvaim. 7He overlaid the temple with gold, its beams, its thresholds, its walls and its doors, and he carved cherubim on the walls.

8He made the most holy place. Its length, matching the width of the temple, was about 30 feet, and its width was about 30 feet. He overlaid it with fine gold weighing about 45,000 pounds. 9The gold for the nails weighed about 1 1/4 pounds. He also overlaid the upper rooms with gold. 10He made two cherubim of sculptured work in the most holy place, and they were overlaid with gold. 11The wings of the cherubim measured about 30 feet in all. One wing of the first cherub, about 7 1/2 feet long, touched the wall of the temple, and its other wing, also about 7 1/2 feet, touched the wing of the second cherub. 12One wing of the second cherub, about 7 1/2 feet long, touched the other wall of the temple, and its other wing, also about 7 1/2 feet, met the wing of the first cherub. 13The wings of these cherubim spread out about 30 feet. They stood on their feet, facing the main hall.

14He made the inner curtain of blue, purple and crimson yarn and fine linen, and worked cherubim into its design.

The two bronze pillars

15In front of the temple he made two pillars about 52 feet long, each with a capital about 7 1/2 feet high on top.

16He made chains in the inner sanctuary and put them on top of the pillars. He also made a hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains. 17He erected the pillars in front of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left. The pillar on the right he named Jachin, and the pillar on the left he named Boaz.
fields.summary: Solomon builds the temple on Mount Moriah, with its most holy place, cherubim, curtain and two pillars.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 4
fields.body_html:
The temple furnishings

1He made a bronze altar about 30 feet long, about 30 feet wide and about 15 feet high.

2He made the Sea of cast metal. It was round, about 15 feet from brim to brim and about 7 1/2 feet high, and it took a line of about 45 feet to measure around it. 3Under its brim were figures of oxen all around it, ten to every 18 inches, encircling the Sea. The oxen were in two rows, cast in one piece with it. 4It stood on twelve oxen: three faced north, three west, three south and three east. The Sea was set on top of them, and their hindquarters were all toward the center. 5It was about 3 inches thick, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It could take in and hold about 18,000 gallons.

6He also made ten basins for washing and put five on the south side and five on the north. In them they rinsed what was used for the burnt offering, but the Sea was for the priests to wash in.

7He made the ten gold lampstands as they were prescribed and put them in the main hall, five along the south side and five along the north.

8He made ten tables and placed them in the main hall, five along the south side and five along the north. He also made one hundred sprinkling bowls of gold. 9He made the court of the priests and the great court, with doors for the court, and he overlaid their doors with bronze. 10He put the Sea on the south side, at the southeast corner. 11Huram also made the pots, the shovels and the sprinkling bowls. So Huram finished the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God: 12the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars; the two networks covering the two bowls of the capitals on top of the pillars; 13the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, in two rows on each network, covering the two bowls of the capitals on top of the pillars; 14the stands, with the basins he made for the stands; 15the one Sea, with the twelve oxen under it; 16and the pots, the shovels and the meat forks. All these things that Huram-abi made for King Solomon for the house of the LORD were of polished bronze. 17The king cast them in the clay ground of the Jordan plain, between Succoth and Zeredah. 18Solomon made all these things in such great numbers that the weight of the bronze was never found out.

The gold furnishings

19Solomon also made all the furnishings of the house of God: the altar of gold; the tables for the bread of the Presence; 20the lampstands and their lamps of pure gold, to burn in front of the inner sanctuary as prescribed; 21the flowers, the lamps and the tongs of gold, the finest gold; 22the wick trimmers, the sprinkling bowls, the dishes and the firepans of pure gold; and the entrance of the house, its inner doors to the most holy place and the doors of the house to the main hall, of gold.
fields.summary: The bronze altar, the sea, the basins, the lampstands and the other furnishings are made.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 5
fields.body_html:
The ark is brought into the temple

1So all the work that Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. Then Solomon brought in the things his father David had dedicated, and he put the silver, the gold and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God.

2Then Solomon called together to Jerusalem the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the ancestral families of the Israelites. They were to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD up from the city of David, that is, Zion. 3All the men of Israel gathered before the king at the festival, which was in the seventh month. 4When all the elders of Israel had arrived, the Levites picked up the ark. 5They brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy utensils that were in the tent. The Levitical priests carried them up. 6King Solomon and the whole congregation of Israel who had gathered to him were in front of the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and cattle that they could not be counted or numbered. 7The priests then carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD into its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, the most holy place, under the wings of the cherubim. 8The cherubim spread their wings over the place where the ark stood, and so the cherubim formed a covering above the ark and its poles. 9The poles were so long that their ends, reaching out from the ark, could be seen in front of the inner sanctuary, though not from outside. It is still there to this day. 10The ark held nothing but the two tablets Moses had put in it at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the Israelites after they came out of Egypt.

The cloud fills the house

11Then the priests came out of the holy place. All the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, whatever their division. 12All the Levites who were singers, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun with their sons and relatives, were standing east of the altar, dressed in fine linen, with cymbals, harps and lyres. With them were 120 priests blowing trumpets. 13The trumpeters and the singers joined as one, making a single sound heard as they praised and thanked the LORD. As they raised the sound with trumpets, cymbals and other musical instruments and praised the LORD, “For he is good; his loyal love lasts forever,” the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud, 14and the priests were unable to stand and do their service because of the cloud, since the house of God was full of the glory of the LORD.
fields.summary: The ark is brought into the most holy place, the singers praise God, and the cloud of God’s glory fills the temple.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 6
fields.body_html:
Solomon speaks to the people

1Then Solomon said,
“The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.
2I myself have built a lofty house for you,
a place for you to dwell forever.”
3Then the king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, while the whole assembly of Israel stood there. 4He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his own mouth made a promise to my father David and with his own hands has now fulfilled it. For he said, 5‘Ever since the day I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I have chosen no city in any tribe of Israel in which to build a house where my name would be, and I have chosen no man to be ruler over my people Israel. 6But I have chosen Jerusalem as the place where my name will be, and I have chosen David to rule over my people Israel.’ 7My father David had it in his heart to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. 8But the LORD said to my father David, ‘You wanted to build a house for my name, and you did well to have this in your heart. 9Yet you are not the one who will build the house. Your son, your own offspring, is the one who will build the house for my name.’ 10Now the LORD has kept the promise he made. I have taken the place of my father David and sit on Israel’s throne, as the LORD promised, and I have built this house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. 11There I have placed the ark, which holds the covenant of the LORD that he made with the Israelites.” 12Then Solomon took his place before the altar of the LORD, in front of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands. 13Solomon had made a bronze platform, about 7 1/2 feet long, about 7 1/2 feet wide and about 4 1/2 feet high, and had set it in the middle of the courtyard. He stood on it, then knelt down in front of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven. 14He said, “The LORD, God of Israel, no God in heaven or on earth is like you. You keep your covenant and show faithful love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart, 15you who have kept for your servant, my father David, the promise you made to him. With your mouth you promised, and with your hand you have fulfilled it, as it is today. 16Now, the LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant, my father David, the promise you made to him: ‘You will never lack a man of your line sitting before me on the throne of Israel, as long as your descendants watch how they live and walk in my law as you have walked before me.’ 17So now, the LORD, God of Israel, let the promise you made to your servant David be confirmed. 18But will God really live on earth with human beings? Heaven itself, even the highest heaven, cannot contain you. How much less this house that I have built! 19Yet listen to the prayer of your servant and to his plea for mercy, the LORD my God. Hear the cry and the prayer that your servant prays before you, 20so that day and night your eyes may be open toward this house, the place where you said you would put your name. Listen to the prayer that your servant prays toward this place. 21Listen to the pleading of your servant and your people Israel as they pray toward this place. Hear from heaven, your dwelling place; and when you hear, forgive. 22When someone sins against a neighbor and is required to take an oath, and comes and swears the oath before your altar in this house, 23then hear from heaven and act. Judge between your servants: repay the guilty by bringing on his own head what he has done, and declare the innocent in the right by rewarding him for his righteousness.

24If your people Israel are defeated by an enemy because they have sinned against you, and they turn back, acknowledge your name, and pray and plead before you in this house, 25then hear from heaven and forgive your people Israel for their sin, and bring them back to the land you gave to them and to their ancestors.

26When the sky is shut and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, and they pray toward this place, acknowledge your name, and turn from their sin because you have humbled them, 27then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, as you teach them the good way to walk in. And send rain on your land, the land you gave to your people as their inheritance.

28If there is famine in the land, or disease, or blight or mildew, locusts or grasshoppers, or if their enemies besiege them in any of their cities, whatever plague or sickness there is, 29whatever prayer or plea for mercy is made by anyone, or by all your people Israel, each one aware of their own affliction and pain and spreading out their hands toward this house, 30then hear from heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive. Give to each one according to all their ways, for you know each heart. You alone know the human heart, 31so that they will fear you and walk in your ways for as long as they live in the land you gave to our ancestors.

32As for the foreigner who is not one of your people Israel but comes from a distant land because of your great name, your mighty hand and your outstretched arm, when they come and pray facing this house, 33then hear from heaven, your dwelling place, and do all that the foreigner asks of you. Then all the peoples of the earth will come to know your name and to fear you as your people Israel do, and to know that your name is called over this house I have built. 34When your people go out to fight against their enemies, wherever you send them, and they pray to you facing this city you chose and the house I built for your name, 35then hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and uphold their cause. 36When they sin against you (and there is no one who never sins), and you are angry with them and hand them over to an enemy, and their captors take them away as prisoners to a land far away or near, 37and they come to their senses in the land where they have been taken captive, and they turn back and plead with you in the land where they are held captive, saying, ‘We have sinned; we have done wrong and acted wickedly,’ 38if they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their captivity, where they were carried off, and pray facing their land, which you gave to their ancestors, and the city you chose, and the house I built for your name, 39then hear from heaven, your dwelling place, their prayer and their pleas, uphold their cause, and forgive your people who have sinned against you. 40Now, my God, please let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer that is prayed in this place.

The prayer closes

41And now rise up, LORD God! Come to the place where you will rest,
you and the ark of your might.
Let your priests, LORD God, be dressed in salvation,
and let those loyal to you rejoice in good things.
42LORD God, do not refuse the kings you have anointed.
Remember the faithful love shown to David your servant.”
fields.summary: Solomon blesses the assembly and prays that God will hear the prayers made toward this house and forgive.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 7
fields.body_html:
Fire from heaven

1As soon as Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and devoured the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the house was filled with the glory of the LORD. 2The priests were unable to enter the house of the LORD, since the house of the LORD was full of the glory of the LORD. 3All the Israelites saw the fire come down and the glory of the LORD over the house, and they knelt with their faces to the ground on the pavement. They worshiped and gave the LORD thanks, for he is good; his loyal love lasts forever. 4Then the king and all the people offered sacrifice before the LORD.

5King Solomon offered as sacrifices 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep. In this way the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. 6The priests stood at their posts, and so did the Levites with the instruments for the LORD’s music that King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD, for his loyal love lasts forever, whenever David offered praise through them. Opposite them the priests sounded the trumpets, and all Israel stood.

7Solomon made holy the central part of the courtyard before the house of the LORD. He offered there the burnt offerings and the fat parts of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold the burnt offerings, the grain offerings and the fat. 8So at that time Solomon held the festival for seven days, and all Israel with him, an enormous assembly from Lebo-hamath to the Wadi of Egypt. 9On the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for they had kept the dedication of the altar for seven days and the festival for seven days. 10On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he let the people go home, joyful and glad at heart for the good the LORD had done for David and for Solomon and for Israel his people. 11So Solomon completed the house of the LORD and the royal palace. Everything he had set his heart on doing in the house of the LORD and in his own palace, he carried out with success.

The LORD appears to Solomon again

12Then during the night the LORD appeared to Solomon. He said to him, “I have heard your prayer, and I have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice. 13When I shut up the sky so that no rain falls, or command locusts to eat up the land, or send a plague among my people, 14and if my people who bear my name humble themselves and pray, seek my face and turn back from their evil ways, then I myself will hear from heaven. I will forgive their sin and heal their land. 15Now my eyes will be open, and my ears will attend to the prayer made in this place. 16Now I have chosen this house and set it apart as holy, so that my name may stay there forever. My eyes and my heart will always be there. 17As for you, if you live before me as your father David did, doing everything I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my rulings, 18then I will make the throne of your kingdom secure, as I promised in my covenant with your father David when I said, ‘There will always be a man of your line ruling in Israel.’ 19But if all of you turn away and abandon my statutes and my commandments that I have set before you, and instead go off to serve other gods and bow down to them, 20then I will uproot them from my land that I have given them, and I will cast this house that I have made holy for my name out of my sight. I will make it a proverb and a byword among all the peoples. 21And this house, high as it once stood, will leave everyone who passes by it appalled. They will ask, ‘Why has the LORD dealt like this with this land and this house?’ 22And people will answer, ‘Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and they embraced other gods and worshiped and served them. That is why he has brought all this disaster on them.’”
fields.summary: Fire comes down from heaven, and God’s glory fills the temple. God appears to Solomon and promises that if the people humble themselves and pray, God will hear and heal their land.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 8
fields.body_html:
Solomon’s building and forced labor

1At the end of the twenty years it took Solomon to build the LORD’s house and his own palace, 2Solomon rebuilt the towns that Huram had given him and settled Israelites in them. 3Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and seized it. 4He built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the store cities that he built in Hamath. 5He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon as fortified towns, with walls, gates and bars, 6and Baalath, all the store cities that Solomon had, all the towns for his chariots and for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout all the land he ruled. 7As for all the people who were left of the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, who were not part of Israel, 8from their descendants who were still left in the land, whom the Israelites had not destroyed, Solomon conscripted forced labor, to this day. 9But Solomon did not make slaves of any of the Israelites for his work. They were his soldiers, the commanders of his officers, and the commanders of his chariots and his horsemen.

10These were King Solomon’s chief officers: 250 of them, who directed the people. 11Solomon moved Pharaoh’s daughter up from the city of David to the house he had built for her. His reason was this: “No wife of mine is to live in the house of David king of Israel, since the places where the ark of the LORD has come are holy.”

Offerings and temple service

12Then Solomon presented burnt offerings to the LORD on the LORD’s altar, which he had built in front of the porch, 13making the offerings each day required, according to the commandment of Moses, on the Sabbaths, at the new moons, and at the appointed festivals three times a year: the Festival of Unleavened Bread, the Festival of Weeks and the Festival of Booths. 14Following the ordinance of his father David, he set the priests in their divisions over their service, and the Levites over their duties of praising and of ministering alongside the priests as each day required, and the gatekeepers by their divisions at each gate. For this was what David the man of God had commanded. 15They did not depart from what the king had commanded the priests and the Levites in any matter, including the treasuries. 16So all Solomon’s work was carried out, from the day the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid until it was finished. The house of the LORD was complete.

Ships to Ophir

17Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and to Eloth, on the seacoast in the land of Edom. 18Huram sent him ships under the command of his own servants, along with servants who knew the sea. They went with Solomon’s servants to Ophir, and brought back from there about 33,750 pounds of gold, which they delivered to King Solomon.
fields.summary: Solomon’s building works, forced labor, worship and trade are described.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 9
fields.body_html:
The queen of Sheba

1The queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s fame, and she came to Jerusalem to test Solomon with difficult questions. She came with a very large company, with camels carrying spices, a great quantity of gold, and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she talked with him about everything she had on her mind. 2Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too hidden for Solomon to explain to her. 3When the queen of Sheba saw Solomon’s wisdom, and the palace he had built, 4the food on his table, the seating of his officials, the service of his attendants and their robes, his cupbearers and their robes, and the burnt offerings he offered at the house of the LORD, she was left breathless. 5She said to the king, “It is true, the report that reached me in my own country about your words and your wisdom. 6But I did not believe what they said until I came and saw it with my own eyes. And indeed, I was not told even half of how great your wisdom is. You go far beyond the report I heard. 7How happy your men must be! How happy are these officials of yours, who stand before you all the time and hear your wisdom! 8Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne as king for the LORD your God! Because your God loves Israel and would make it stand firm forever, he has made you king over them, to do justice and righteousness.” 9Then she gave the king about 9,000 pounds of gold, a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. No spices ever matched those that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. 10Huram’s servants and Solomon’s servants, who brought gold from Ophir, brought algum wood from there too, and precious stones. 11The king used the algum wood to make steps for the house of the LORD and the royal palace, as well as lyres and harps for the singers. Nothing like them had ever been seen before in the land of Judah. 12King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and asked for, more than she had brought to the king. Then she turned and went back to her own country, she and her servants.

Solomon’s wealth

13The weight of the gold that came to Solomon in one year was about 50,000 pounds of gold, 14not counting what the traveling traders and the merchants brought in. All the kings of Arabia, and the governors of the land as well, brought gold and silver to Solomon. 15King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold, with about 15 pounds of beaten gold going into each shield. 16He also made 300 shields of beaten gold, with about 7 1/2 pounds of gold going into each shield. The king placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

17Then the king made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with pure gold. 18The throne had six steps and a footstool of gold, fastened to the throne. On either side of the seat were armrests, with two lions standing beside the armrests. 19Twelve lions stood there on the six steps, one at each end of each step. Nothing like it had ever been made for any kingdom. 20All King Solomon’s drinking cups were gold, and all the utensils in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. In Solomon’s days silver was not thought of as anything. 21For the king had ships that sailed to Tarshish with Huram’s servants. Once every three years the Tarshish ships would come in, bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks.

22So King Solomon grew greater in riches and in wisdom than all the kings of the earth. 23All the kings of the earth sought an audience with Solomon, to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. 24Each of them brought a gift: articles of silver and gold, robes, weapons and spices, horses and mules, so much every year.

The end of Solomon’s reign

25Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and he had 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. 26He ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and as far as the border of Egypt. 27The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore-fig trees of the Shephelah. 28Horses were brought for Solomon from Egypt and from all the lands. 29The rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are written in the records of Nathan the prophet, in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer about Jeroboam son of Nebat. 30Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years. 31Then Solomon rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David his father. And his son Rehoboam became king in his place.
fields.summary: The queen of Sheba visits Solomon and praises his wisdom, and his wealth and fame are described. Solomon dies after reigning forty years.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 10
fields.body_html:
Israel rejects Rehoboam

1Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had gathered at Shechem to make him king. 2When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about it, he was in Egypt, where he had taken refuge from King Solomon, and he returned from Egypt. 3So they sent and summoned him, and Jeroboam and all Israel came and said to Rehoboam, 4“Your father made our yoke hard. Now ease the harsh labor your father demanded and the heavy yoke he laid on us, and we will serve you.” 5He said to them, “Come back to me in three days.” So the people left.

6King Rehoboam then consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon while he was alive. “What answer do you advise me to give this people?” he asked. 7They answered him, “If you are kind to this people and show them favor, and speak kind words to them, they will always be your servants.” 8But he rejected the advice the elders had given him and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and now served him. 9He asked them, “What do you advise? How should we answer this people who have said to me, ‘Lighten the yoke your father put on us’?” 10The young men who had grown up with him answered, “The people said to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you must make it lighter for us.’ Give them this answer: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist. 11So then: my father laid a heavy yoke on you, but I will make your yoke heavier still. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.’”

The harsh answer

12On the third day Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam, as the king had told them: “Return to me on the third day.” 13The king gave them a harsh answer. King Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders. 14He spoke to them as the young men had advised: “I will make your yoke heavy, and I will add to its weight. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.” 15So the king did not listen to the people, for this turn of events came from God, so that the LORD might fulfill the word he had spoken to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the Shilonite.
16When all Israel saw that the king would not listen to them, the people answered the king:
“What part do we have in David?
We have no inheritance in Jesse’s son!
Each man to your tents, Israel! Now look after your own house, David!”
So all Israel went home.

17But Rehoboam reigned over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah. 18King Rehoboam then sent Hadoram, the officer over the forced labor, but the Israelites stoned him to death. King Rehoboam managed to get up into his chariot and escape to Jerusalem.

19So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.
fields.summary: Rehoboam refuses to lighten the people’s burdens, and Israel rebels and makes Jeroboam king.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 11
fields.body_html:
Shemaiah forbids war

1When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he mustered the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 picked warriors, to fight against Israel and regain the kingdom for Rehoboam.

2But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God: 3“Speak to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin, and tell them, 4‘The LORD says this: Do not go up to fight against your relatives. Go home, every one of you, for this thing has come from me.’” So they heeded the words of the LORD and turned back from marching against Jeroboam.

Rehoboam fortifies Judah

5Rehoboam stayed in Jerusalem and built up cities in Judah for defense. 6He fortified Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, 7Beth-zur, Socoh, Adullam, 8Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, 9Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, 10Zorah, Aijalon and Hebron, fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin. 11He strengthened the fortresses and put commanders in them, with stores of food, oil and wine. 12In every city he placed large shields and spears and made the cities very strong. So Judah and Benjamin remained his.

Priests and Levites come to Judah

13The priests and the Levites who lived throughout Israel took their stand with him, coming from all their territories. 14The Levites left their pasturelands and their property and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons had cast them out of their service as priests of the LORD. 15He appointed his own priests for the high places, for the goat-demons and for the calves he had made. 16Following them, people from all the tribes of Israel who had set their hearts on seeking the LORD, the God of Israel, came to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their ancestors. 17They gave strength to the kingdom of Judah and stood by Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years, since for three years they walked in the way of David and Solomon. 18Rehoboam married Mahalath, whose father was Jerimoth son of David and whose mother was Abihail daughter of Eliab son of Jesse. 19She bore him sons: Jeush, Shemariah and Zaham. 20After her he married Maacah daughter of Absalom, and she bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza and Shelomith. 21Rehoboam loved Maacah daughter of Absalom more than all his other wives and concubines. He had taken eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters. 22Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maacah as chief, the ruler among his brothers, because he intended to make him king. 23He acted wisely: he dispersed some of his sons throughout all the districts of Judah and Benjamin, to all the fortified cities. He gave them plenty of provisions and sought many wives for them.
fields.summary: Rehoboam fortifies Judah, and priests and Levites from the north come to him. His family is listed.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 12
fields.body_html:
Shishak invades Judah

1When Rehoboam’s kingdom was firmly established and he had become strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him.

2In King Rehoboam’s fifth year, because they had broken faith with the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, 3with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen, and troops beyond counting came with him from Egypt: Libyans, Sukkiim and Cushites. 4He took the fortified cities belonging to Judah and advanced as far as Jerusalem.

5Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the officials of Judah, who had gathered at Jerusalem for fear of Shishak, and said to them, “The LORD says this: You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to Shishak.” 6Then the officials of Israel and the king humbled themselves. “The LORD is righteous,” they said. 7When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, a word from the LORD came to Shemaiah: “They have humbled themselves, so I will not destroy them. I will grant them some deliverance, and my wrath will not be poured out on Jerusalem through Shishak. 8Yet they will become his servants, so that they may learn what it is to serve me and what it is to serve the kingdoms of other lands.”

9So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He carried off the treasures of the house of the LORD and those of the king’s palace. He took everything, even the gold shields Solomon had made. 10King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and entrusted them to the commanders of the guard who kept watch at the entrance of the king’s palace. 11Whenever the king went into the house of the LORD, the guards came and carried the shields, and afterward they brought them back to the guardroom. 12Because he humbled himself, the anger of the LORD turned back from him and did not destroy him completely. And there were also good things in Judah.

The end of Rehoboam’s reign

13King Rehoboam established himself firmly in Jerusalem and reigned. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen from among all the tribes of Israel as the place for his name. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite. 14He did what was evil, because he had not set his heart on seeking the LORD.

15The acts of Rehoboam, from first to last, are written in the records of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer, in the genealogical records. There were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually. 16Rehoboam rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David. His son Abijah became king in his place.
fields.summary: Rehoboam abandons God’s law, and Shishak of Egypt attacks Jerusalem. When the leaders humble themselves, God spares them from destruction.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 13
fields.body_html:
Abijah king of Judah

1In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah became king over Judah. 2He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam. 3Abijah went into battle with an army of warriors, 400,000 chosen men, and Jeroboam drew up his battle lines against him with 800,000 chosen men, mighty warriors.

Abijah’s speech on Mount Zemaraim

4Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim, in the hill country of Ephraim, and said, “Listen to me, Jeroboam and all Israel! 5Should you not know that the LORD, the God of Israel, gave the kingship over Israel to David and his sons forever by a covenant of salt?

6Yet Jeroboam son of Nebat, an official of Solomon son of David, rose and turned in revolt against his own master. 7Worthless men, scoundrels, gathered around him and stood firm against Rehoboam son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and timid and could not hold his own against them. 8And now you mean to stand against the kingdom of the LORD that David’s sons hold. You are a vast horde, and with you are the golden calves Jeroboam made to be your gods. 9Did you not drive out the priests of the LORD, Aaron’s sons, together with the Levites, and make your own priests as the peoples of other lands do? Anyone who comes to consecrate himself with a young bull and seven rams becomes a priest of what are no gods.

10But we have the LORD as our God, and we have not forsaken him. Sons of Aaron serve the LORD as priests, and the Levites are at their work. 11Every morning and every evening they burn burnt offerings and fragrant incense to the LORD. The bread is set out in rows on the pure table, and the lamps on the golden lampstand are lit every evening. For we are keeping the charge of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him. 12Look, God is with us at our head, and his priests are here with their trumpets to sound the battle call against you. Israelites, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your ancestors, for you will not succeed.” 13Meanwhile Jeroboam had sent an ambush around to come up behind them, so that his army was in front of Judah and the ambush was behind them. 14When Judah turned, they saw that the battle was in front of them and behind them. They cried out to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets. 15Then the men of Judah raised the battle cry. And as they shouted, God struck down Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. 16The Israelites fled before Judah, and God gave them into Judah’s hands. 17Abijah and his troops struck them with a great slaughter, and 500,000 chosen men of Israel fell dead. 18So the Israelites were humbled at that time, and the men of Judah won the day, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their ancestors. 19Abijah pursued Jeroboam and took towns from him: Bethel and the villages around it, Jeshanah and its villages, and Ephron and its villages. 20Jeroboam did not regain his power during the days of Abijah. The LORD struck him, and he died.

The end of Abijah’s reign

21But Abijah grew strong. He took fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.

22The rest of the acts of Abijah, his ways and his words, are written in the commentary of the prophet Iddo.
fields.summary: Abijah of Judah faces Jeroboam in battle and declares that God is with Judah, and Judah wins.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 14
fields.body_html:
Asa king of Judah

1Then Abijah rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa became king in his place. In his days the land had peace for ten years.

2Asa did what was good and right in the sight of the LORD his God. 3He took away the foreign altars and the high places, smashed the standing stones and cut down the Asherah poles. 4He commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their ancestors, and to carry out the law and its commands. 5He removed the high places and the incense altars from all the cities of Judah, and the kingdom had peace under him. 6He built fortified cities in Judah, since the land had peace. No one went to war with him in those years, because the LORD had given him rest. 7He said to Judah, “Let us build these cities and put walls around them, with towers, gates and bars. The land is still ours, for we have sought the LORD our God. We sought him, and he gave us rest all around.” So they built, and they prospered.

Victory over Zerah the Cushite

8Asa had an army of 300,000 men from Judah, armed with large shields and spears, and 280,000 from Benjamin, who carried small shields and drew the bow. All of them were mighty warriors. 9Zerah the Cushite marched out against them with an army of a million men and 300 chariots, and he came as far as Mareshah. 10Asa went out to meet him, and they took up their positions for battle in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah. 11Then Asa cried out to the LORD his God: “LORD, there is no one but you to help when the weak stand against the strong. Help us, LORD our God, because we are depending on you; it is in your name that we have marched out against this huge army. LORD, you are our God. Let no mortal hold out against you.”

12The LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and before Judah, and the Cushites fled. 13Asa and the troops with him chased them as far as Gerar. So many Cushites fell that they could not recover; they were shattered before the LORD and his army. The men of Judah carried off a great deal of plunder. 14They attacked all the cities around Gerar, for the dread of the LORD lay on them. They plundered all those cities, since there was a great deal of plunder in them. 15They also attacked the herders’ camps and carried off sheep and goats in great numbers, and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.
fields.summary: Asa removes foreign altars and idols and seeks God, and defeats Zerah the Cushite.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 15
fields.body_html:
Azariah’s message to Asa

1The Spirit of God came on Azariah son of Oded. 2He went out to meet Asa and spoke to him: “Hear me, Asa, and all of Judah and Benjamin. The LORD is with you as long as you are with him. If you seek him, he will let you find him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you.

3Israel went a long time without the true God, without a priest to teach, and without law. 4But in their distress they turned back to the LORD the God of Israel; they sought him, and he let them find him. 5In those times there was no peace for anyone who went out or came in, because great turmoil troubled all who lived in those lands. 6Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, because God troubled them with every kind of distress. 7But as for you, be strong and do not let your hands go slack, for your work will be rewarded.”

Asa renews the covenant

8When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he gathered his courage. He removed the detestable idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the towns he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim, and he repaired the altar of the LORD that stood in front of the porch of the LORD’s temple. 9He assembled all Judah and Benjamin, and the people from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon who were living among them as outsiders. Great numbers had deserted to him from Israel, because they saw that the LORD his God was with him.

10They assembled at Jerusalem in the third month of Asa’s fifteenth year as king. 11On that day they sacrificed to the LORD from the plunder they had brought back: 700 cattle and 7,000 sheep. 12They entered into the covenant: they would seek the LORD, the God of their ancestors, with all their heart and with all their soul, 13and anyone, young or old, man or woman, who refused to seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death. 14They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice, with shouts of joy, and with trumpets and rams’ horns. 15All Judah rejoiced over the oath, because they had sworn it with all their heart and had sought him with all their desire, and he let them find him. So the LORD gave them rest on every side. 16King Asa even deposed his mother Maacah as queen mother, because she had made a horrid image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image, crushed it and burned it in the Kidron Valley. 17The high places, however, were not taken away from Israel. Even so, Asa’s heart was undivided all his life. 18He brought into the house of God the gifts his father had dedicated and the gifts he himself had dedicated: silver, gold and utensils. 19There was no war until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa.
fields.summary: The prophet Azariah urges Asa to seek God, and Asa leads a covenant renewal and removes his grandmother as queen mother.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 16
fields.body_html:
Asa’s treaty with Aram

1In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah, to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah. 2Then Asa brought out silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king’s palace, and sent it to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who ruled in Damascus, with this message: 3“Let there be a treaty between you and me, as there was between my father and your father. I am sending you silver and gold. Go and break off your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, and he will withdraw from me.” 4Ben-hadad agreed with King Asa and sent the commanders of his forces out against the cities of Israel. They conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim and all the store cities of Naphtali. 5When Baasha heard about it, he stopped building Ramah and abandoned his work.

6Then King Asa brought all Judah, and they carried away the stones and timber Baasha had used to build Ramah. With them he fortified Geba and Mizpah.

Hanani rebukes Asa

7At that time the seer Hanani came to Asa king of Judah and told him, “You relied on the king of Aram and did not rely on the LORD your God. Because of that, the army of the king of Aram has slipped out of your hand. 8Were not the Cushites and the Libyans a huge army, with chariots and horsemen in great numbers? But you relied on the LORD, and so he handed them over to you. 9For the eyes of the LORD roam over all the earth, so that he may show his strength for those whose hearts are undivided toward him. You have acted foolishly in this matter, and from this time on you will face wars.” 10Asa was angry with the seer and put him in prison in the stocks, because he was furious with him over this. And at that time Asa dealt harshly with some of the people. 11The acts of Asa, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. 12Asa’s feet became diseased in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, and the disease grew very severe. Even in his sickness he did not seek the LORD; he sought only the physicians. 13Then Asa rested with his ancestors; he died in the forty-first year of his reign. 14They buried him in his own tomb, which he had hewn for himself in the City of David, and laid him on a bier filled with spices and many kinds of perfumes blended by the perfumer’s art. And they made a very great fire in his honor.
fields.summary: Asa hires the king of Aram against Israel instead of relying on God, imprisons the seer who rebukes him, and in his illness seeks only physicians.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 17
fields.body_html:
Jehoshaphat king of Judah

1His son Jehoshaphat became king in his place, and he made himself strong against Israel. 2He stationed troops in every fortified city of Judah, and he placed garrisons in the land of Judah and in those Ephraimite towns his father Asa had taken. 3The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he followed the earlier ways of his ancestor David and did not seek the Baals, 4but sought the God of his father and followed his commandments, and did not act as Israel did. 5The LORD made the kingdom secure under his rule. All Judah brought gifts to Jehoshaphat, and he had great riches and honor. 6His heart was bold in the ways of the LORD, and he also removed the high places and the Asherah poles from Judah.

Teaching the law in Judah

7In the third year of his reign he sent out his officials to teach in the cities of Judah: Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel and Micaiah. 8With them were the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah and Tob-adonijah, and with them the priests Elishama and Jehoram. 9They taught in Judah, having the book of the law of the LORD with them. They went around to all the cities of Judah and taught the people. 10The dread of the LORD was on all the kingdoms of the lands around Judah, so they did not go to war against Jehoshaphat. 11Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat gifts and silver as tribute, and the Arabs also brought him flocks: 7,700 rams and 7,700 male goats.

Jehoshaphat’s army

12Jehoshaphat grew steadily more and more powerful, and he built fortresses and store cities in Judah. 13He had large supplies in the cities of Judah, and soldiers, mighty warriors, in Jerusalem. 14This was their muster by ancestral families. From Judah, the commanders of thousands: Adnah was the commander, and he had 300,000 mighty warriors with him,

15next to him was Jehohanan the commander, and with him 280,000,

16next to him was Amasiah son of Zichri, who had volunteered himself for the LORD, and with him 200,000 mighty warriors.

17From Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty warrior, and with him 200,000 men armed with bow and shield,

18next to him was Jehozabad, and with him 180,000 men armed for war.

19These were the men who served the king, besides those he had stationed in the fortified cities throughout Judah.
fields.summary: Jehoshaphat strengthens Judah, follows God and sends officials and Levites to teach the law in every town.

fields.title: 2 Chronicles 18
fields.body_html:
Micaiah prophesies against Ahab

1Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab. 2Some years later he went down to visit Ahab in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered sheep and cattle in great numbers for him and for the people who were with him, and he urged him to go up against Ramoth-gilead. 3Ahab king of Israel asked Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Will you come with me to Ramoth-gilead?” He replied, “I am as you are, and my troops are as your troops. We will be with you in the battle.” 4But Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “First, please seek the word of the LORD.” 5So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, four hundred men, and asked them, “Shall we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I hold back?” “Go up,” they said, “for God will give it into the king’s hand.” 6But Jehoshaphat said, “Is there no other prophet of the LORD here whom we can ask?” 7The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man through whom we could inquire of the LORD: Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him, for his prophecies about me are never good, but always bad.” Jehoshaphat said, “Let the king not speak like that.” 8So the king of Israel called one of his court officials and said, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.” 9Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, dressed in their royal robes. They were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance to the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying in front of them. 10Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made himself iron horns, and he said, “The LORD says this: ‘With these you will gore the Arameans until they are destroyed.’” 11All the prophets were prophesying the same thing: “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and be victorious. The LORD will give it into the king’s hand.” 12The messenger who had gone to call Micaiah said to him, “Listen, the prophets are all speaking with one voice, and what they say is good for the king. Please let your word be like one of theirs, and speak favorably.” 13But Micaiah said, “As surely as the LORD lives, whatever my God says is what I will speak.” 14When he came to the king, the king asked him, “Micaiah, shall we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I hold back?” He answered, “Go up and be victorious. They will be given into your hand.” 15But the king said to him, “How often must I put you under oath to tell me only the truth in the name of the LORD?”
16Then Micaiah said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills,
like sheep that have no shepherd.
And the LORD said, ‘These have no master;
let each of them go home in peace.’”
17The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not say to you that he prophesies nothing good about me, only bad?”

18Micaiah went on, “Then hear the word of the LORD. I saw the LORD seated on his throne, with all the host of heaven standing at his right and at his left. 19The LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab king of Israel to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ Some suggested one thing and some another. 20Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD and said, ‘I will entice him.’ The LORD asked him, ‘How?’ 21He said, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ The LORD said, ‘You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go and do it.’ 22So now, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these prophets of yours. The LORD has decreed disaster for you.”
